title: Soil, Peat, Coco and Soilless Media Properties

content.overview: Root-zone media differ in particle structure, water retention, aeration, drainage, cation interactions, biological activity, and stability. A medium should be managed according to its actual physical and chemical behavior rather than its marketing category alone.

vocabulary.definition: A root substrate formulated without field soil, commonly using materials such as peat, coco coir, bark, perlite, or mineral components.
The amount of water retained by a medium after drainage under defined conditions.
The fraction of pore volume occupied by air after excess water has drained.

sections.title: Particle structure controls pore space
sections.body: Large and small particles create different pore-size distributions. Those pores determine how quickly water drains, how much remains available, and how much air remains around roots after irrigation.

sections.title: Organic and inert media behave differently
sections.body: Peat, coco, bark, mineral aggregates, and field soils have different physical stability and chemical interactions. Management should account for these differences rather than applying one irrigation schedule to every substrate.

sections.title: Container geometry changes effective behavior
sections.body: The same medium can hold water differently in shallow and tall containers because gravitational drainage and the perched water region depend on container dimensions.

workedExamples: A peat-heavy mix and a coarse coco-perlite mix may require different irrigation frequencies even when plants are the same size.
If a shallow container stays wetter than expected, consider container geometry as well as the recipe.
The same coco product behaves differently after repeated compression and reuse because pore structure changes; irrigation should follow measured behavior, not the label.
Two containers use the same mix, but the shorter/wider container retains a larger saturated zone than the taller one. Container geometry changes effective drainage.
commonMistakes: Assuming all coco products or all soils behave identically.
Choosing irrigation frequency without observing actual dryback.
Ignoring compaction and media breakdown over time.
Assuming media labels predict exact water-air behavior without measurement.
Ignoring container height when comparing drainage.
content.practicalApplication: Record the media composition, container geometry, drainage behavior, saturation duration, and crop response. Use those observations to set irrigation frequency rather than copying a schedule from a different substrate system.
content.summary: Media choice creates the physical environment around roots. Water retention, aeration, drainage, chemistry, and container geometry determine how that medium should be managed.

blocks.title: Media create the physical root environment
blocks.body: Particle size, pore distribution, organic matter, mineral components and compaction determine how water and air occupy the container after irrigation. The medium name is less important than its measured physical behavior.

blocks.title: Media properties that change management
rows: Different wetness in shallow vs tall pots

left.label: Fine/high-retention mix
left.body: Slower drainage, more retained water, potentially longer interval between irrigations.

right.label: Coarse/high-aeration mix
right.body: Faster drainage, more air-filled pore space, potentially more frequent irrigation.

blocks.title: Compare two media systems
blocks.instructions: Use weight, drainage time and moisture data for two substrate/container combinations.
prompts: How does container geometry affect the result?
What irrigation-frequency difference would you test?

blocks.title: Key takeaway
blocks.body: Manage the root zone from measured physical behavior, not from the media name alone.
